Adult hooknose (Agonus cataphractus) are relatively small benthic fishes inhabiting the northeastern Atlantic, and their life-history metrics reflect a slow-paced strategy typical of cold-water sculpins. Field surveys indicate that sexual maturity is attained at a relatively modest body size, with individuals beginning to reproduce once they reach a standard length of approximately six centimeters [Lp = approximately six centimeters]. At this size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is calculated to be roughly 2.17 grams [Wwp = roughly 2.17 grams], a value that aligns closely with the morphometric relationships established for the species. Measurements taken during the peak spawning period at a stable water temperature of 9.2 °C [T = 9.2 °C] yielded a mean gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 10% [GSI = 10%].

Eggs deposited during the winter months experience a prolonged incubation period before the emergence of the yolk-sac larva; at a constant temperature of 9.2 °C [T = 9.2 °C], the age at birth — defined as the moment of chorion rupture and larval eclosion — was recorded as thirty days [ab = thirty days]. This protracted incubation interval is attributable to the low metabolic rates imposed by the cold environment, which slows the rate of enzymatic cleavage and organogenesis within the developing teleost embryo. The newly emerged prolarva is minuscule, possessing an initial wet weight at birth of just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a value derived from an average egg diameter of two millimeters. This minute size necessitates an extended period of dependence on endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding, during which the alevin undergoes significant allometric growth.

Growth curve analyses from long-term mark-recapture studies indicate that the asymptotic or ultimate standard length for this species is twenty-one centimeters [Li = twenty-one centimeters]. Converting this length measurement using the established length-weight relationship yields a corresponding ultimate wet weight of approximately 92 grams [Wwi = approximately 92 grams], representing the maximum body mass typically recorded for fully grown, reproductively active adults. This modest adult size places the species in a low-intermediate position within the trophic guild of North Sea benthic predators, limiting the range of prey sizes it can exploit and making it vulnerable to piscine and avian predators throughout its life. The slow approach to this asymptote, combined with the delayed maturation noted earlier, contributes to a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survivorship over rapid somatic growth.

Longevity records for hooknose, derived from analysis of otolith annuli and validated by captive holding studies at a controlled temperature of 9.2 °C [T = 9.2 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 1095 days [am = approximately 1095 days], corresponding to roughly three years. Instead, females appear to maintain a consistent annual reproductive output, iteroparity being favored over a single, high-fecundity spawning event given the environmental predictability of their cold-water habitat.

Comparative studies with other Northeastern Atlantic cottids highlight the conservative life-history strategy of Agonus cataphractus. The size at which 50% of individuals are mature, a standard length of approximately 6 centimeters [Lp = approximately 6 centimeters], is proportionally larger relative to ultimate length than observed in sympatric species such as Myoxocephalus scorpius, indicating a later onset of reproduction.
